meta.title_plain: How a carpenter's wooden duck led to the LEGO brick
meta.teaser: Ole Kirk Christiansen turned a struggling woodshop into the company behind your favourite bricks.

page.title: How a carpenter's wooden duck led to the LEGO brick
page.sub: The story of Ole Kirk Christiansen and the birth of LEGO
page.bigIdea: Ole Kirk faced hard times, doubting relatives and a factory fire. He kept going because he believed only the best is good enough for kids.

cards.title: A boy who loved wood
cards.front: Ole Kirk was born in Denmark in 1891. He was one of 13 kids.
cards.back: His family was poor, and he worked on farms as a young boy. He loved whittling wood. In 1916 he bought a carpentry shop in Billund.
cards.tryit: Build a tiny workshop with a workbench and one tool in 10 minutes.

cards.title: Hard times, new idea
cards.front: In the early 1930s, few people could afford his ladders and ironing boards.
cards.back: So he started making cheap wooden toys. When yo-yos stopped selling, he cut them in half and used them as wheels for toy cars!
cards.tryit: Build a pull-along toy car using only the bricks you find in 5 minutes.

cards.title: Two words, one name
cards.front: His toy company needed a name. He played with two Danish words.
cards.back: "Leg godt" means "play well" in Danish. He joined the first letters: LE + GO. The name LEGO was born in the mid-1930s.
cards.tryit: Build the word LEGO, or your own name, with bricks in under 15 minutes.

cards.title: The duck that taught quality
cards.front: His son Godtfred once saved money by giving toy ducks two coats of varnish, not three.
cards.back: Ole made him fetch the ducks back and add the last coat, alone, even if it took all night. The motto became "Only the best is good enough."
cards.tryit: Build a duck in 10 minutes. Then spend 5 more making one detail better.

cards.title: From wood to plastic
cards.front: In 1942 a fire destroyed his factory. He rebuilt it for his workers.
cards.back: In 1947 he bought a plastic-moulding machine that cost over twice the year's profit. Plastic bricks followed, and the brick design was patented in 1958.
cards.tryit: Test clutch power: stack 2x4 bricks into a tower. How tall before it wobbles?

words.d: A person who builds and fixes things made of wood.
A clear coating that makes wood shiny and protects it.
A short saying that sums up what someone believes.
Pressing hot, melted plastic into a shape, then letting it cool.
The grip that holds two LEGO bricks firmly together.

quiz.q: What did Ole Kirk do when yo-yos stopped selling?
opts: Cut them in half to make toy car wheels
quiz.hint: Think about what round, flat shapes could help a toy move.
quiz.why: He reused the yo-yos as wheels, so nothing went to waste.

quiz.q: What does "leg godt" mean in Danish?
quiz.hint: It's about what kids do with toys.
quiz.why: "Leg godt" means "play well," and LEGO comes from its first letters.

quiz.q: Why did Godtfred have to fetch the ducks back?
opts: They were missing a coat of varnish
quiz.hint: Count the coats: how many did they usually get?
quiz.why: He skipped the third coat, and his dad wanted every toy done properly.

quiz.q: What does Ole Kirk's story teach about setbacks?
opts: Only work when things are easy
quiz.hint: Think about the fire and the hard 1930s. What did he do each time?
quiz.why: He rebuilt after a fire and kept trying new ideas, like plastic bricks.

page.think: Ole Kirk said only the best is good enough. What's one thing, in tennis or building, where you could add your own "third coat"?
